0.title: Setup
0.md:
- **Time-box / lane:** ~2 h fast lane — test-out gate first (`fast-lane-protocol.md`)
- Compiler toolchain: gcc or clang, understand what "compile then link" means
- `make` basics: targets, dependencies, a Makefile for a 2-file program
- `gdb`: breakpoint, step, print, backtrace
- Editor/LSP: clangd or ccls wired up
- Project: hand-compile and hand-link a 2-file "hello" program without an IDE button

1.title: C Basics
1.md:
- **Time-box / lane:** ~4 h fast lane — test-out gate first (`fast-lane-protocol.md`)
- Types, `sizeof`, two's-complement integer representation, IEEE-754 float layout
  (sign/exponent/mantissa — why `0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3`), overflow behavior
- Control flow, functions, pass-by-value
- Arrays, C strings (`char*`, null termination), `<string.h>`
- `printf`/`scanf` format strings and their footguns
- Errors to practice: type-mismatch/format-string warnings — and, deliberately, the
  *absence* of an error on out-of-bounds array access. First lesson: "it compiled and
  ran" proves nothing.
- Project: a CLI tool that parses argv and does basic string processing (e.g. word count)

2.title: The Memory Model
2.md:
- **Time-box / lane:** ~14 h fast lane — test-out gate first (`fast-lane-protocol.md`)
- Stack vs heap, what a stack frame actually is
- Pointers: declaration, dereference, pointer arithmetic, pointer vs array decay
- `malloc`/`calloc`/`realloc`/`free`, and every way to leak or double-free
- Structs, unions, `typedef`
- Struct memory layout: field ordering, padding, alignment — why `sizeof(struct)` isn't
  the sum of its fields, and how reordering fields can shrink it
- Function pointers
- Real-world: this is literally what allocators inside Redis/game engines do — see
  `tutorials/real-world.md`
- Errors to practice: segfault + `gdb bt`, Valgrind "invalid read/write," glibc "double
  free or corruption" abort
- Efficiency: start the *measure it* habit here, don't wait for Phase 9's `perf`. Time a
  stack-allocated loop vs the same loop heap-allocating each iteration with `malloc`,
  with a plain wall-clock timer. See the gap for real before reasoning about why it
  exists.
- **Fun project (optional, alongside the graded project below): "Pointer Maze."**
  Pointers are THE iconic C difficulty — make it a game instead of a slog. Build a
  terminal maze where the maze itself is a pointer-linked graph (each cell `malloc`'d,
  linked to its neighbors via pointers), navigate it live, then add a "break it" mode
  that deliberately dangles or double-frees a cell — run it under ASan/UBSan and watch
  the exact bug you just wrote get caught in real time.
- Project: a manually-managed dynamic array (resizable "vector") in raw C

3.title: Multi-File C
3.md:
- **Time-box / lane:** ~10 h fast lane — test-out gate first (`fast-lane-protocol.md`)
- Headers, include guards, declaration vs definition
- `static`, linkage (internal/external), the "linker error" categories
- Static vs dynamic libraries (`.a` / `.so`), how `#include` differs from linking
- Preprocessor: macros, conditional compilation, why macros are usually the wrong answer
- Bitwise ops, flags, bit-packed structs
- File I/O (`fopen`/`fread`/`fwrite`, buffered vs unbuffered)
- Errors to practice: linker errors (`undefined reference to`, `multiple definition of`)
  vs compiler errors — telling the two categories apart on sight is the actual skill
- Project: split the Phase 2 dynamic-array into a proper `.h`/`.c` library, linked into a
  second program

**Checkpoint — jump-off point for DSA.** Pointers, structs, and manual memory are solid
enough to start [[DSA]] here if you want to interleave. Come back for Phase 4+ later.

**Also the earliest reasonable point for a scoped capstone attempt** — a C-only
version of Phase 9's capstone (skip concurrency, skip custom allocators) is genuinely
attemptable from here. The full capstone wants Phase 5+ if you want it in C++ with
RAII; it's fine to attempt the C version now and redo it in C++ later once that's
solid, rather than waiting for Phase 9 to exist as a concept at all.

4.title: C Systems Programming
4.md:
- **Time-box / lane:** ~12 h fast lane — test-out gate first (`fast-lane-protocol.md`)
- Processes: `fork`/`exec`/`wait`, exit codes
- Syscalls vs libc wrappers, `strace` to see the boundary
- Signals: `SIGSEGV`, `SIGINT`, handlers, why signal handlers are dangerous
- Undefined behavior: what the standard actually leaves undefined, and why "it worked on
  my machine" is not evidence of correctness
- Tooling: Valgrind (memcheck), AddressSanitizer/UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer
- Standard-library headers worth knowing beyond STL containers: `<chrono>` (durations/
  clocks with actual type safety, not raw milliseconds as an `int`), `<filesystem>`
  (portable path/directory handling, no more hand-rolled `#ifdef _WIN32` path code)
- Errors to practice: `Segmentation fault (core dumped)` from a raw signal, ASan/UBSan
  structured reports, reading `strace` output
- Project: a tiny shell that forks, execs a command, and waits on it

5.title: C++ Fundamentals (arriving from C)
5.md:
- Companion reading (after your own attempt, never first): `~/ElementalMedia/spectate/CPlusPlusThings/basic_content/` (Light-City — C++ internals Q&A style: `this`, `static`, `const`, references, virtual tables, memory layout). Use for interview-style self-quizzing; the mentor still teaches mechanism-first.
- **Time-box / lane:** ~6 h fast lane — test-out gate first (`fast-lane-protocol.md`)
- What C++ adds over C: references, function overloading, namespaces, `bool`, `new`/`delete`
- Classes: constructors, destructors, member functions, `this`
- Const-correctness: `const` references/parameters, const member functions — a
  compile-time contract the compiler enforces, not a style suggestion
- RAII — the single most important idea in C++: tie resource lifetime to object lifetime
- Errors to practice: "no matching function for call to" — first taste of
  overload-resolution errors; and silent object slicing (no error at all — another
  "compiled and ran" trap)
- Project: reimplement the Phase 2 dynamic array as a C++ class with RAII (no manual free
  calls at the call site)

6.title: C++ OOP
6.md:
- **Time-box / lane:** ~10 h fast lane — test-out gate first (`fast-lane-protocol.md`)
- Inheritance, virtual functions, vtables (know what's happening under the hood)
- Abstract base classes / interfaces
- Operator overloading, when it helps vs when it obscures
- Real-world: vtable dispatch is how every game engine's entity/component system and
  every plugin architecture routes calls at runtime
- **Design patterns, named explicitly:** Adapter (a class wrapping an incompatible
  interface, exposing the one your code expects, without touching what's wrapped) —
  Dependency Injection (a constructor takes a base-class pointer/reference, not a
  concrete type — swap the real implementation for a test double without the class
  knowing; direct parallel to what [[Python]]'s `Protocol`-typed constructors do)
- Errors to practice: pure-virtual-call abort (`pure virtual method called`), ambiguous-
  base errors from diamond inheritance
- Project: a small shape hierarchy with virtual `area()`, driven polymorphically through a
  base-class pointer/reference

7.title: Generic Programming & STL
7.md:
- **Time-box / lane:** ~13 h fast lane — test-out gate first (`fast-lane-protocol.md`)

Templates get equal billing with STL here, not a footnote — the STL is templates.

- Templates: function templates, class templates, template specialization, a light
  touch of SFINAE (enough to recognize it in library code, not to write it fluently yet)
- STL containers (`vector`, `map`, `unordered_map`, `set`), iterators, algorithms header
- Exceptions: `try`/`catch`/`throw`, `noexcept`, when C++ code should throw vs return an
  error code, and how RAII destructors interact with stack unwinding during a throw
  (what happens to a `unique_ptr` member when its owning object's constructor throws
  partway through?)
- Errors to practice: a template error wall — long, nested, misleading-looking; the
  skill is finding the one real line in the noise, not reading top to bottom — and an
  uncaught exception's `terminate() called after throwing... what():` message
- **Fun project (optional, alongside the graded project below): "Build Your Own
  `variant`."** Templates/SFINAE are this language's second-most notorious wall after
  pointers — build a tiny type-safe tagged union from scratch with templates, before
  you ever see `std::variant` in Phase 8. Then deliberately misuse your own template
  (wrong type, missing specialization) to trigger a real template error wall on
  purpose, and practice finding the one real line in the noise.
- Project: reimplement one STL algorithm (e.g. `std::sort` on a small scale) to understand
  what the abstraction is hiding. Compare after with `~/ElementalMedia/spectate/C-Plus-Plus` (TheAlgorithms — clean C++ implementations of sorts/searches/data structures; read-only, diff your version, don't copy; pairs with [[DSA]] Ph1–6)
- **Library reading #1 — Catch2** (`~/ElementalMedia/spectate/Catch2`, header-style test framework, templates + macros + expression decomposition): write the project's self-check as a Catch2 `TEST_CASE` instead of `assert.h` (allowed from here; `assert.h` stays valid). Then read how `REQUIRE(a == b)` captures both sides via expression templates — the real-world payoff of this phase's template material.
- Companion reading: `~/ElementalMedia/spectate/CPlusPlusThings` (STL, `effective_cpp`, templates sections) and the Phase 7 chapters of `~/ElementalMedia/spectate/modern-cpp-tutorial` (Changkun — `book/en-us/04-containers.md`). This fills the gap noted under Video references: no local video course covers templates/STL.

8.title: Modern C++ (11/14/17/20)
8.md:
- **Time-box / lane:** ~12 h fast lane — test-out gate first (`fast-lane-protocol.md`)
- Smart pointers: `unique_ptr`, `shared_ptr`, `weak_ptr` — RAII generalized
- Move semantics: rvalue references, `std::move`, why copies were expensive before this
- Lambdas, `auto`, structured bindings, `std::function`/`std::bind` (a callable that
  can hold a function pointer, a lambda, or a bound member — C++'s equivalent of
  treating functions as values, direct parallel to [[Python]]'s HOF material)
- **`std::optional`/`std::variant`** — C++'s answer to the nullable/sum-type question:
  `optional<T>` instead of a sentinel value or a raw pointer meaning "maybe null,"
  `variant<A, B, C>` as a type-safe union (the compiler enforces you handle every
  case via `std::visit`, unlike a raw C `union`). Direct parallel worth naming: this
  is the same job [[Python]]'s `typing.Optional`/`typing.Union` do, enforced by the
  compiler here instead of a separate type checker.
- `constexpr`, ranges (17/20 as relevant)
- Errors to practice: use-after-move (usually no error, just wrong behavior — the Phase
  1 "no error ≠ correct" lesson again) and a dangling reference to a local (sometimes
  warned, often not)
- Project: rewrite the Phase 6 shape hierarchy using smart pointers, no raw `new`/`delete`
  anywhere in user code
- **Primary text for this phase: `~/ElementalMedia/spectate/modern-cpp-tutorial`** (Changkun, C++11→26): `book/en-us/02-usability.md` (auto, constexpr, structured bindings, `nullptr`), `03-runtime.md` (lambdas, `std::function`, rvalue refs/move), `05-pointers.md` (smart pointers); `10-cpp20.md`–`12-cpp26.md` are skim-only extensions (concepts, ranges, coroutines, modules). Do its `exercises/` and run its `code/` per chapter — type them yourself first, diff after.
- **Library reading #2 — nlohmann/json** (`~/ElementalMedia/spectate/json`, `include/nlohmann/json.hpp`): idiomatic modern C++ API design — implicit conversions, `operator[]`, initializer lists, SFINAE-based `to_json`/`from_json` ADL customization points, `basic_json` as a heavily templated type. Trace one call (`j["a"] = 1;` and `j.get<T>()`) end to end with the Reading Unfamiliar Code workflow (`learning-toolkit-protocols.md`). Goal is to *recognize* the patterns from Ph7, not rewrite them.

9.title: Master
9.md:
- **Time-box / lane:** ~22 h fast lane — test-out gate first (`fast-lane-protocol.md`)
- Concurrency: `std::thread`, mutexes, atomics, data races, why locking is hard
- **Fun project (optional, alongside the capstone below): "Dining Philosophers
  Simulator."** Concurrency is C++'s other famous hard spot — the classic CS puzzle
  makes it visible instead of abstract. Terminal-visualize N philosophers each
  needing two fork mutexes to eat; run it naively and watch it deadlock on screen;
  fix it with a resource-ordering rule (or a waiter/arbitrator) and watch the
  deadlock disappear for real, not just in a description.
- **Library reading #3 — spdlog** (`~/ElementalMedia/spectate/spdlog`): production library design — sink abstraction (runtime polymorphism where it's cheap), `fmt` formatting, async logger (bounded MPMC queue + worker thread, overflow policy), thread-safe vs `_st` sink variants (mutex cost chosen at the type level). Map each design decision to this phase's concurrency material; measure sync vs async throughput yourself (`perf`/timer), don't trust the README.
- Concurrency companion: `~/ElementalMedia/spectate/CPlusPlusThings/concurrency/`; tests of your capstone in Catch2 (concurrency tests: run under TSan).
- Custom allocators, placement `new`
- Profiling: `perf`, understanding cache behavior, why "big O" isn't the whole story —
  the full triad is correctness, then memory footprint, then measured speed, in that
  order, and "measured" means `perf`/a timer, never guessed
- Errors to practice: a TSan race-condition report, and a deadlock — no error at all,
  just a hang; the final and hardest form of "silence is not proof of correctness"
- **This is the "cracked at C/C++" project** — the thing that proves it, not another
  exercise. See Phase 3's checkpoint above for the earliest reasonable attempt if you
  haven't already.
- Capstone project (pick one): a toy `malloc` implementation, a bytecode VM, a small
  multithreaded work-queue, a tiny in-memory key-value store with a raw-socket TCP
  interface (Redis-shaped), or a **thread-safe LRU cache** — take the sequential
  hashmap+doubly-linked-list version [[DSA]] already builds and make it
  production-grade: a `std::mutex` (or `shared_mutex` for read-heavy workloads)
  guarding it, a benchmark showing throughput under contention with N threads
  hammering `get`/`put` concurrently — something that forces memory model + concurrency + design
  together. See `tutorials/real-world.md` for where each of these shows up for real.

10.title: Maverick
10.md:
Master proves you're solid across the whole language. Maverick is a chosen
specialization on top of that — pick one track below (or more than one), not all
four are required. Each track's project sits at the same bar as Phase 9's capstone:
scoped one level deeper into a real domain, not another exercise.

### Track A — Embedded/Firmware
- RTOS internals: task scheduling, priority inversion, ISR-safe code (no `malloc`, no
  blocking calls in an interrupt handler)
- Direct register access vs HAL: reading a datasheet, memory-mapped peripheral
  registers, `volatile` and why the compiler can't be trusted to leave hardware reads
  alone
- Interrupt-driven drivers vs polling, DMA basics
- Errors to practice: a missing `volatile` optimized away (no error, wrong behavior —
  another "compiled and ran" trap), a priority-inversion deadlock, a stack overflow on
  a tiny embedded stack (silent corruption, not a clean segfault like Phase 2's)
- Project: an interrupt-driven driver (UART or SPI) with correct ISR/task handoff,
  replacing a polling version if Phase 4's course built one
- Course: `~/ElementalMedia/Courses/IoT/[FreeCourseSite.com] Udemy - Mastering Microcontroller with Embedded Driver Development` (deeper than Phase 4's bare-metal intro); `~/ElementalMedia/Courses/IoT/Advanced Embedded Systems with Arduino` for a second angle — neither content-verified against this track yet, folder names only

### Track B — High-Performance / Low-Latency
- SIMD intrinsics (SSE/AVX), when the compiler auto-vectorizes and when it won't
- Lock-free data structures: atomics beyond Phase 9's basics, memory ordering
  (`memory_order_relaxed`/`acquire`/`release`), the ABA problem
- Cache-line awareness: false sharing, padding, structure-of-arrays vs
  array-of-structures for hot loops
- Errors to practice: a false-sharing benchmark regression (no error, just a number
  that's mysteriously worse across threads — profiling as debugging, not `gdb`), a
  lock-free structure that passes single-threaded tests and fails under load (a race
  no test caught — Phase 9's TSan lesson again, but harder to provoke on purpose)
- Project: take Phase 9's capstone thread-safe LRU cache (if built with a mutex) and
  build a lock-free variant, or a lock-free single-producer/single-consumer queue —
  benchmark both under contention, numbers or it didn't happen
- No course/book in the library covers SIMD/lock-free/low-latency profiling directly —
  nothing to point to. Lean on Phase 9's `perf` habit and "C++ Concurrency in Action"'s
  atomics/memory-order chapter as the foundation, then go primary-source (compiler
  intrinsics docs, `perf stat`/`perf record` output) for the rest

### Track C — Security / Reverse Engineering
- Stack/heap overflow mechanics: how a buffer overflow overwrites a return address, why
  ASLR/stack canaries/NX exist and what each actually stops
- Reading disassembly: `objdump`/`gdb`'s `disassemble`, recognizing a function
  prologue/epilogue, calling conventions at the assembly level
- Fuzzing your own code: point a fuzzer (AFL++ or libFuzzer) at a Phase-2-era program
  with a deliberately reintroduced bug, watch it find the crash you already know is
  there
- Errors to practice: a fuzzer-found crash with a minimized reproducer, a
  stack-smashing detection abort (`*** stack smashing detected ***`), reading a raw
  disassembly listing with no source alongside it
- Project: deliberately write a small vulnerable C program (stack overflow, off-by-one),
  exploit it yourself locally (shellcode or return-to-libc, whatever your toolchain
  allows), then patch it and confirm the same input no longer works — offense then
  defense, on code you wrote and understand fully
- Course: `~/ElementalMedia/Courses/Developer/Reverse Engineering 4 -  Software Protection` — not content-verified against this track yet, folder name only

### Track D — C++ ↔ Python Bridge
- **Time-box:** ~12 h
- Pairs with [[Python]] Phase 10 Track A (same boundary, other side). Bind a small C++ class + function set into a Python module with **pybind11** (`~/ElementalMedia/spectate/pybind11`; `docs/basics.rst`, `docs/classes.rst`): templates doing the type-conversion work, the GIL (`py::gil_scoped_release` around long C++ work), ownership across the boundary (return-value policies, `py::keep_alive`), buffer protocol/NumPy zero-copy, ABI/compiler-version matching between the built `.so` and the Python interpreter.
- Errors to practice: a dangling reference returned to Python after the C++ owner died (use-after-free surfaced as a Python crash/garbage), a C++ exception crossing the boundary (maps to a Python exception — check what), an `ImportError` from ABI/Python-version mismatch, GIL not released so a Python thread pool gains nothing.
- Project: take Phase 9's thread-safe LRU cache (or Phase 7's algorithm) → importable Python module with a `pytest` suite and a benchmark vs the pure-Python/`functools.lru_cache` version, numbers shown.
- Course: none in the library — primary sources are the pybind11 docs and its `tests/`.

0.title: Setup
0.md:
- **Time-box / lane:** ~2 h fast lane — test-out gate first (`fast-lane-protocol.md`)
- Confirm C/C++ comfort: pointers, structs, arrays, `malloc`/`free` (C-Cpp Phase 2–3).
  Shaky here → go there first, come back.
- Pick a build/test loop for tiny algorithm programs (single-file + `gcc`/`g++`, or a
  minimal Makefile) — don't over-build tooling for this.
- Project: none — this phase is a readiness check, not content.

1.title: Algorithm Analysis & Recursion (book ch. 1–2)
1.md:
- **Time-box / lane:** ~8 h fast lane — test-out gate first (`fast-lane-protocol.md`)
- Variables, data types, data structures, ADTs — vocabulary, not just definitions
- What is an algorithm; why analyze algorithms at all
- Asymptotic notation: Big-O, Omega (Ω), Theta (Θ) — what each actually bounds
- Master Theorem (divide-and-conquer recurrences) + the subtract-and-conquer variant
- Amortized analysis — why a sequence of operations can be cheap even if one op is
  expensive
- Recursion: call stack visualization, recursion vs iteration trade-offs
- Backtracking: what makes a problem backtracking-shaped
- Errors to practice: stack overflow from unbounded or wrong-base-case recursion
- Project: hand-trace (on paper) the recursion tree for a non-trivial recursive
  function before running it; then implement one classic backtracking problem
  (N-Queens or subset-sum) from scratch

2.title: Linear Structures (book ch. 3–5)
2.md:
- **Time-box / lane:** ~14 h fast lane — test-out gate first (`fast-lane-protocol.md`)
- Linked lists: singly, doubly, circular, memory-efficient doubly (XOR trick), unrolled,
  skip lists — and a direct comparison against arrays/dynamic arrays
- Stacks: ADT, array vs linked-list implementation, real applications (expression eval,
  backtracking support)
- Queues: ADT, implementation, applications
- Real-world: doubly linked list + hash table (Phase 6) is the classic LRU cache combo —
  see `tutorials/real-world.md`
- Errors to practice: null-pointer dereference on empty-list edge cases — the head/tail
  off-by-one that every list operation has to handle
- Efficiency: this is where Phase 1's amortized analysis stops being abstract — a
  dynamic array's doubling strategy is the concrete case. And Big-O alone doesn't pick
  a winner here: linked list is O(1) insert but pointer-chasing kills cache locality;
  array is O(n) insert but contiguous in memory. State both the complexity AND the
  memory-access pattern before calling one "better."
- Project: implement singly + doubly linked list, stack, and queue from raw pointers
  (no `std::`), each with the chapter's "Problems & Solutions" attempted

3.title: Trees, Heaps, Disjoint Sets (book ch. 6–8)
3.md:
- **Time-box / lane:** ~14 h fast lane — test-out gate first (`fast-lane-protocol.md`)
- Binary trees: types, properties, traversals (pre/in/post/level-order), generic
  (N-ary) trees
- Threaded binary trees (stack/queue-less traversal), expression trees, XOR trees
- Binary Search Trees, balanced BSTs, AVL trees (rotations)
- Priority Queues / Heaps: heap property, binary heap, heapsort connection
- Disjoint Sets ADT: union-find, fast UNION vs fast FIND trade-offs
- Real-world: heaps back OS schedulers and Dijkstra's frontier; union-find backs
  Kruskal's MST and Git-style merge-set detection — see `tutorials/real-world.md`
- Errors to practice: stack overflow on deep unbalanced-tree recursion, null-child
  dereference
- **Fun project (optional, alongside the graded project below): "AVL Tree Animator."**
  Rotations are famously fiddly to get right by hand — make them visible instead of
  something you simulate on paper. Build a terminal visualizer that draws the tree
  live as you insert values, triggers a rotation the moment balance breaks, and
  redraws the rebalanced tree so you watch it happen instead of trusting the code.
- Project: BST with insert/delete/search + all four traversals; a binary heap with
  sift-up/sift-down; union-find with path compression

4.title: Graph Algorithms (book ch. 9)
4.md:
- **Time-box / lane:** ~14 h fast lane — test-out gate first (`fast-lane-protocol.md`)
- Graph representation: adjacency list vs matrix, when each wins
- Traversals: BFS, DFS, and what each is actually good for
- Topological sort
- Shortest path algorithms (Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford as the book covers)
- Minimal Spanning Tree (Prim's/Kruskal's)
- Real-world: BFS → social network "friends of friends"; topo-sort → why `npm install`/
  `make` can run at all; shortest-path → the algorithm behind "shortest route" in maps
- Errors to practice: infinite loop from a missing visited-check — a hang, not a crash,
  the DSA version of "silence is not proof of correctness" — plus stack overflow on deep
  DFS
- **Fun project (optional, alongside the graded project below): "Pathfinding
  Visualizer."** Graphs are a common early wall — this is one of the most satisfying,
  well-known project shapes for a reason. Race BFS/DFS/Dijkstra/A* live on a terminal
  grid maze, watch each algorithm's frontier expand differently, and see exactly why
  Dijkstra explores more than A* on the same maze instead of taking it on faith.
- Project: adjacency-list graph with BFS, DFS, topological sort, and one shortest-path
  algorithm, run against a hand-drawn graph you trace by hand first

5.title: Sorting, Searching, Selection, Symbol Tables (book ch. 10–13)
5.md:
- **Time-box / lane:** ~12 h fast lane — test-out gate first (`fast-lane-protocol.md`)
- Sorting: bubble, selection, insertion, shell, merge, heap, quick, tree sort — plus
  linear-time sorts (counting, bucket/bin, radix) and when comparison-based sorting's
  Ω(n log n) floor doesn't apply
- External sorting (data bigger than memory) — concept level
- Searching: linear, sorted/ordered linear, binary, interpolation
- Selection algorithms: partition-based selection, median-of-medians (linear selection)
- Symbol tables: what they are, implementation trade-offs
- Errors to practice: off-by-one bounds in binary search (wrong answer or infinite loop,
  not a crash), quicksort's worst-case stack overflow on already-sorted input
- Efficiency: quicksort is in-place (O(1) extra space) but O(n²) worst case; mergesort
  is O(n log n) guaranteed but needs O(n) extra space. Two separate axes — memory and
  time — not one ranking; state both before picking one over the other for a given case.
- Project: implement quicksort and mergesort from scratch, state and verify their
  complexity (best/avg/worst), implement binary search + one selection algorithm

6.title: Hashing & String Algorithms (book ch. 14–15)
6.md:
- **Time-box / lane:** ~10 h fast lane — test-out gate first (`fast-lane-protocol.md`)
- Hashing: hash table ADT, hash functions, load factor, collision resolution (separate
  chaining, open addressing), bloom filters, when hashing is the wrong tool
- String matching: brute force, Rabin-Karp, KMP, Boyer-Moore
- Data structures for strings: tries, ternary search trees, suffix trees — trade-offs
  between BSTs/tries/TSTs for storing strings
- Real-world: tries back autocomplete/spell-check/IP-routing longest-prefix-match; hash
  tables back every DB index and cache — see `tutorials/real-world.md`
- Errors to practice: off-by-one in a hash function's modulo, buffer overrun in raw
  C-string handling
- Efficiency: load factor is a direct memory-for-speed trade — a higher load factor
  wastes less memory but lengthens collision chains (slower lookups); a lower one is
  faster but wastes space. Name the number, don't just say "resize when it gets full."
- Project: a hash table with chaining from scratch; KMP string matcher; a trie with
  insert/search/prefix-search; once Phase 2's doubly linked list exists, combine it with
  this phase's hash table into an LRU cache — O(1) get/put with eviction

7.title: Algorithm Design Techniques (book ch. 16–19)
7.md:
- **Time-box / lane:** ~18 h fast lane — test-out gate first (`fast-lane-protocol.md`)
- Classification of algorithm design techniques (by implementation method, by design
  method)
- Greedy: what makes greedy work, when it doesn't, classic greedy problems
- Divide and Conquer: the pattern, when it always/never applies, connection back to the
  Master Theorem from Phase 1
- Dynamic Programming: properties required (optimal substructure, overlapping
  subproblems), greedy vs divide-and-conquer vs DP, top-down vs bottom-up, Longest
  Common Subsequence as the canonical worked example
- Errors to practice: memo-table index-out-of-bounds, and recognizing exponential
  blowup — a brute-force solution that's simply still running, not crashed, on an input
  one size bigger than yesterday's
- **Fun project (optional, alongside the graded project below): "DP Table Animator."**
  DP is the book's own hardest chapter and the topic most cited as DSA's hardest,
  period — make the "aha" visible instead of abstract. Build a terminal visualizer
  that animates a memoization table filling in real time for a chosen problem (coin
  change or LCS), racing it live on-screen against the brute-force version's runtime
  on the same input — watch the exponential blowup and the DP fix happen side by side.
- Project: one problem solved three ways where applicable (brute force → greedy or DC →
  DP) to feel the actual trade-off, not just read about it; LCS implemented from scratch

8.title: Complexity Classes & Master Capstone (book ch. 20–21)
8.md:
- **Time-box / lane:** ~14 h fast lane — test-out gate first (`fast-lane-protocol.md`)
- Complexity classes: polynomial vs exponential time, decision problems, decision
  procedures, P/NP framing, reductions
- Miscellaneous: bit-manipulation hacks, the book's "other programming questions" grab-bag
- **This is the "cracked at DSA" project** — the real test, not another drill. A
  scoped version (skip Phase 7-8 topics, pull hard problems only from Phases 2-6) is
  genuinely attemptable once Phase 5 (sorting/searching) is solid — don't wait for all
  8 phases to exist as a concept before finding out where you actually stand.
- The priority-queue (Phase 3) + topological-sort (Phase 4) combo you've already
  built separately is exactly what a dependency-aware task scheduler needs — see
  [[Golang]] Phase 9 if the full running system (not just the algorithms) is wanted.
- Capstone: a timed mixed problem set, one hard problem pulled from each earlier phase
  (mock-interview style) — the real test of whether structures/algorithms transfer under
  pressure, not just in isolation right after reading the chapter

9.title: Maverick
9.md:
- **Time-box / lane:** optional, uncounted

Master proves you're solid across the whole book. Maverick is a chosen specialization
beyond it — pick a track (or several), not all are required. Tracks below are ordered
easiest/smallest-scope → hardest/largest-scope; each track's project sits at the same
bar as Phase 8's capstone, not another exercise. None of these come from the book —
this phase is explicitly beyond-the-book territory, same spirit as `real-world.md`'s
existing "beyond this book: B-trees, Red-Black trees" callout.

### Track A — String Algorithms at Scale
- Suffix arrays (construction, and what they answer that a suffix tree also answers
  but with a smaller constant), the Z-algorithm (linear-time pattern matching,
  contrast against Phase 6's KMP — same asymptotic class, different mechanism)
- Aho-Corasick: multi-pattern matching in one pass — the actual algorithm behind
  "search for these 500 words in this text at once," not 500 separate KMP passes
- Errors to practice: an off-by-one in suffix-array construction that silently
  produces a valid-looking but wrong sorted order (wrong output, not a crash — this
  vault's main failure mode, now one level deeper than Phase 6's basic string bugs),
  an Aho-Corasick trie with a missing failure link that causes a match to be
  silently skipped
- Efficiency: Aho-Corasick is O(n + m + z) for text length n, total pattern length
  m, matches found z — state why that beats m separate O(n) KMP passes for m
  patterns, don't just assert it's faster
- Project: implement the Z-algorithm and Aho-Corasick from scratch, benchmark
  Aho-Corasick against Phase 6's KMP run m times on the same multi-pattern search,
  show the crossover point where Aho-Corasick wins
- No course in the library — nothing to point to. CLRS's string-matching chapter
  and the original Aho-Corasick paper are the standard primary sources

### Track B — Advanced Data Structures Beyond the Book
- Direct continuation of the gap `real-world.md` already names: B-trees/B+trees
  (what every real database index actually is — contrast against Phase 3's binary
  BST: why a wide, shallow tree wins when each node read is a disk seek, not a
  cache-line fetch), Red-Black trees (a different self-balancing strategy than
  Phase 3's AVL — color-based rotation rules instead of height-balance rotation
  rules)
- Persistent/immutable data structures: a structure where "modifying" it returns a
  new version without mutating the old one (structural sharing, not a full copy) —
  the mechanism behind Git's own object model and Clojure's core data types
- Errors to practice: a B-tree split/merge that leaves the tree's own invariant
  broken (wrong output on the next lookup, not a crash — the exact same
  silent-wrong-output failure mode this whole vault trains for, now on a harder
  structure), a "persistent" structure that accidentally mutates shared state
  anyway (breaks the old version too — the bug defeats the entire point of the
  structure, and nothing crashes to reveal it)
- Efficiency: a B-tree's branching factor is chosen around disk-block/page size
  specifically to minimize seeks — state the actual number (order 100+ is common),
  not just "wide is better"
- Project: implement a B-tree (insert/delete/search, with real split/merge on
  overflow/underflow) and a Red-Black tree (insert with rotations + recoloring)
  from scratch, each with a test proving the invariant holds after a long random
  sequence of operations
- No course in the library — nothing to point to. CLRS's B-tree and Red-Black tree
  chapters are the standard primary source

### Track C — Advanced Graph Algorithms
- Max-flow/min-cut (Ford-Fulkerson, and why the max-flow value always equals the
  min-cut capacity — not a coincidence, a theorem)
- Strongly connected components (Tarjan's or Kosaraju's) — what "strongly
  connected" means beyond Phase 4's plain connectivity, and why it matters (cycle
  detection at scale, dependency-graph analysis beyond a simple DAG)
- A* in depth (beyond Phase 4's fun-project intro): heuristic admissibility, why an
  inadmissible heuristic can make A* return a wrong (non-shortest) answer with zero
  error — this vault's failure mode again, now in a pathfinding context
- Errors to practice: an inadmissible A* heuristic silently producing a suboptimal
  path (wrong output, no crash, no warning — the actual danger of "it found *a*
  path" being mistaken for "it found *the* path"), a Ford-Fulkerson implementation
  that loops forever on a graph with real-valued (not integer) capacities using the
  naive augmenting-path choice (a correctness edge case the book's Phase 4 material
  never has to confront)
- Project: implement Ford-Fulkerson from scratch on a small flow network, verify
  max-flow equals min-cut by computing both independently; implement Tarjan's SCC
  and A* with both an admissible and a deliberately-inadmissible heuristic, showing
  the wrong-answer case side by side with the correct one
- No course in the library — nothing to point to. CLRS's flow-networks and SCC
  chapters, and the original A* paper (Hart/Nilsson/Raphael), are the standard
  primary sources

### Track D — Computational Geometry
- Convex hull (Graham scan or divide-and-conquer) — a genuinely different problem
  shape than anything in the book: geometric, not purely combinatorial
- Closest-pair-of-points (the divide-and-conquer version, direct callback to Phase
  1's Master Theorem material — a real application of the pattern beyond sorting)
- Line-sweep as a technique: why sweeping a line across a plane turns a 2D
  geometric problem into a sequence of 1D events processed in order
- Errors to practice: a convex-hull implementation that mishandles collinear
  points (wrong hull shape, no crash — geometry's own flavor of silent wrong
  output), a floating-point comparison bug in an orientation test (two points that
  should be exactly collinear compare as "almost" collinear due to float error — a
  correctness class this vault hasn't had to deal with since everything else has
  been discrete/integer-based)
- Project: implement convex hull and the divide-and-conquer closest-pair algorithm
  from scratch, on both a hand-constructed small case (verified by hand) and a
  large random point set (cross-checked against a brute-force O(n²) closest-pair)
- No course in the library — nothing to point to. CLRS's computational geometry
  chapter and "Computational Geometry: Algorithms and Applications" (de Berg et
  al.) are the standard primary sources

### Track E — Nearest-Neighbor & Similarity Search
- KD-trees: a BST-shaped structure (direct extension of Phase 3) but splitting on
  alternating dimensions instead of one key — what "nearest neighbor" even means as
  a query type, distinct from Phase 3's exact-match search
- Approximate nearest neighbor (ANN): why exact NN degrades toward brute-force in
  high dimensions (the "curse of dimensionality," a real named failure mode of
  KD-trees specifically) and why approximate methods trade exactness for speed on
  purpose
- Locality-sensitive hashing (LSH): hashing designed so *similar* inputs collide
  more often, not less — the direct inversion of Phase 6's hash-table goal
  (minimize collisions) into a genuine feature this time
- Errors to practice: a KD-tree nearest-neighbor query that returns a wrong
  (non-nearest) point because a pruning decision was too aggressive (wrong output,
  no crash, and it's *close* to right which makes it easy to miss), an LSH
  implementation with a hash-family choice that doesn't actually satisfy the
  locality-sensitive property (looks like it works on a small test set, silently
  degrades on real high-dimensional data)
- Project: implement a KD-tree with real nearest-neighbor query, benchmark it
  against brute-force linear scan as dimensionality increases and show the curse of
  dimensionality actually happening (the crossover point where KD-tree stops
  winning); implement a small LSH scheme and verify empirically that similar
  inputs collide more than dissimilar ones
- No course in the library — nothing to point to. This is also the direct
  algorithmic core behind [[Python]] Maverick Track F's (Data Science/ML)
  similarity/recommendation work, if that vault's Maverick phase is in play — name
  the connection if it's live

### Track F — Randomized & Approximation Algorithms
- Randomized quicksort's *formal* expected-case analysis (Phase 5 covered the
  practical worst-case-on-sorted-input problem; this is the probabilistic proof of
  why random pivoting fixes it in expectation, not just empirically)
- Approximation algorithms for NP-hard problems: a real approximation ratio (e.g. a
  2-approximation for vertex cover), what "guaranteed within 2x of optimal" buys
  you once Phase 8 already established the exact problem is intractable at scale
- Monte Carlo vs Las Vegas algorithms as a named distinction — one trades
  correctness for speed with a bounded error probability, the other trades speed
  for guaranteed correctness (randomized quicksort is Las Vegas; a randomized
  primality test like Miller-Rabin is Monte Carlo)
- Errors to practice: an approximation algorithm's output silently exceeding its
  proven approximation ratio because of an implementation bug (not a runtime error
  — the number is simply wrong relative to the guarantee, and nothing checks that
  at runtime for you), a Monte Carlo algorithm's false-positive/negative rate not
  actually matching its theoretical bound because the random source itself is
  flawed (a bad RNG, not a bad algorithm)
- Project: implement a 2-approximation for vertex cover (or another classic
  approximation algorithm) and empirically verify its ratio against optimal on
  small graphs (small enough to brute-force the true optimum for comparison);
  implement Miller-Rabin primality testing and empirically measure its actual
  false-positive rate against the theoretical bound
- No course in the library — nothing to point to. CLRS's randomized-algorithms
  and approximation-algorithms chapters are the standard primary sources

### Track G — System-Design-Scale Application
- Direct extension of the cross-links this syllabus already names ([[Golang]]
  Phase 9's Task Scheduler, [[Python]]'s capstones) — but now the algorithm choice
  IS the design decision being evaluated, mock-system-design-interview style, not
  just "implement X"
- A rate limiter: token bucket vs sliding window vs fixed window — three different
  data-structure choices for the same problem, each with a different
  correctness/memory trade-off under concurrent access
- A distributed cache or URL shortener at the depth Phase 8's capstone already
  gestures at, but now with the underlying structure choice (consistent hashing for
  cache sharding, a specific hash+base62 scheme for the shortener) stated and
  defended against at least one alternative
- Errors to practice: a sliding-window rate limiter that's subtly wrong at window
  boundaries (allows a burst right at the boundary that a correct implementation
  wouldn't — wrong output under a specific timing condition, not caught by a
  simple single-request test), a consistent-hashing scheme with too few virtual
  nodes causing uneven load distribution (correct in the sense that it "works,"
  wrong in the sense that one node gets hammered — a load-imbalance bug that only
  shows up under real traffic patterns, not a unit test)
- Project: design and implement one system (rate limiter, distributed cache shard
  router, or URL shortener) with the underlying algorithm/structure choice
  explicitly justified against one alternative, plus a test that specifically
  targets the boundary/edge case named above for whichever system is chosen
- No course in the library — nothing to point to. System-design-interview
  references (widely available "system design primer" style write-ups) are the
  primary source, alongside this syllabus's own existing [[Golang]]/[[Python]]
  cross-links

### Track H — Parallel/Distributed Algorithms
- Largest, most novel scope of any track here — correctness under
  concurrency/failure is a different discipline than anything Phase 0-8 trained
  for, closer to [[Golang]] Phase 6's concurrency material than to anything in
  this book
- Parallel sorting and MapReduce-shaped algorithm design: how a sequential
  algorithm's structure has to change to actually parallelize (not just "run it on
  multiple cores and hope"), the shuffle/reduce step's own cost
- Consensus algorithms (Raft or Paxos, at a conceptual level): why "just have
  everyone agree" is genuinely hard once nodes can fail or messages can be
  delayed/lost — the actual reason distributed systems are a distinct discipline,
  not just "regular systems but bigger"
- Errors to practice: a naive parallel-sort merge step that's correct sequentially
  but produces wrong output under real parallel execution because of a missing
  synchronization point (a race, not a crash — the same class of bug [[Golang]]
  Phase 6 trains for, now in an algorithmic context instead of a systems one), a
  simplified consensus implementation that appears to work in every test run
  until a deliberately-injected node failure or message delay exposes a
  split-brain scenario (two nodes both believe they're the leader — no error
  anywhere, just silently incoherent global state)
- Project: implement a parallel merge sort (real concurrency, not a simulated
  split) with a race-free test; implement a simplified single-decree Paxos or
  Raft leader-election protocol and deliberately inject a node failure or network
  delay to trigger and observe a split-brain scenario before fixing it
- No course in the library — nothing to point to. The original Raft paper ("In
  Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm," Ongaro & Ousterhout) and
  Lamport's Paxos writings are the standard primary sources

0.title: What a Container Actually Is
0.md:
- A container is a Linux process with namespaces (pid, net, mnt, uts, ipc, user) and
  cgroups (CPU/memory limits) on a layered filesystem (overlayfs)
- VM vs container: shared kernel, what that means for isolation and startup time
- Docker architecture: CLI → `dockerd` → `containerd` → `runc`; images vs containers;
  registries
- Linux primer only if needed: processes, permissions, env vars (Mosh course lessons
  11–27)
- Errors to practice: `permission denied ... docker.sock` (why, and why the `docker`
  group is root-equivalent), `Unable to find image ... locally`, `port is already
  allocated`
- Project: run `nginx` detached, find its PID on the host, list its namespaces under
  `/proc/<pid>/ns`, compare with a host shell's; cap its memory with `--memory` and
  watch it OOM with a stress command

1.title: Images & Dockerfiles
1.md:
- Layers: each instruction → a layer; content-addressed; the build cache and what
  invalidates it (order instructions: deps before source)
- Build context and `.dockerignore` (why `node_modules`/`.venv`/`.git` must not go in)
- `FROM` choice (`python:3.12-slim` vs `alpine` + musl gotchas), `COPY` vs `ADD`, `RUN`,
  `ENV`/`ARG` (build-time vs run-time), `EXPOSE` (documentation only!), `USER`,
  `WORKDIR`
- `ENTRYPOINT` vs `CMD`, exec form vs shell form (preview of Phase 2's PID 1 problem)
- Tagging and pushing; `docker history`, `dive`
- Errors to practice: `COPY failed: file not found in build context`, a cache miss on
  every build because `COPY . .` comes before `pip install`, running as root and
  `docker exec whoami`
- Efficiency: measure build time cold vs warm-cache; image size per layer
- Project: Dockerize a Django app (gunicorn), cache-friendly, non-root user, with
  `.dockerignore`

2.title: Containers at Runtime
2.md:
- Volumes vs bind mounts vs tmpfs — where data actually lives on the host
- Networking: default bridge vs user-defined bridge (DNS by container name), `-p`
  publishing, `host` network; `localhost` inside a container is the container itself
- Logs (stdout/stderr → log driver), `exec`, `inspect`, restart policies, resource limits
- **Mechanism anchor — PID 1 and signals:** `docker stop` sends SIGTERM to PID 1, waits
  10s, then SIGKILL; shell-form `CMD` makes `/bin/sh` PID 1 and swallows the signal;
  `exec` form, `exec "$@"` in entrypoint scripts, `--init`/tini
- Errors to practice: container exit code 137 (OOM or SIGKILL — tell which from
  `inspect`), `could not connect to server` from app → `localhost:5432`, a bind mount
  hiding the image's files
- Project: Postgres with a named volume surviving `docker rm`; a Django container that
  shuts down gracefully in <1s (prove it with timing), and one that doesn't — explain
  the difference

3.title: Docker Compose
3.md:
- Services, networks, volumes in one file; `docker compose up/down/logs/exec/run`
- `depends_on` + `condition: service_healthy` + healthchecks — "started" ≠ "ready"
- Config: `.env`, `env_file`, secrets (and why env vars leak), profiles, override files
  (`compose.override.yaml` for dev, a prod file without bind mounts)
- The career-plan dev stack: Django + Postgres + Redis + Celery worker + Celery beat
- Running migrations and tests inside the stack
- Errors to practice: app starts before Postgres accepts connections, two services on
  the same host port, a volume holding stale data after a schema change
- Project: `docker compose up` → working Django app with Postgres, Redis, Celery; a
  `check.sh` that brings it up, hits a health endpoint, enqueues a Celery task, asserts
  it ran, tears down

4.title: Production Images
4.md:
- Multi-stage builds: build deps in one stage, copy only artifacts into a slim final
  stage; distroless images
- Size budgets, `--mount=type=cache` (BuildKit) for pip, reproducible builds, pinning
  base images by digest
- `HEALTHCHECK`, read-only root filesystem, dropping capabilities, non-root
- Scanning: `trivy image` — reading CVE output, what's fixable vs noise
- Errors to practice: a multi-stage build missing a runtime shared library
  (`ImportError: libpq.so.5`), a distroless image with no shell to debug (how *do* you
  debug it?)
- Efficiency: final image size before/after, build time with/without cache mounts
- Project: production image under a size budget you set, zero HIGH/CRITICAL fixable
  CVEs, healthcheck, non-root — `check.sh` asserts all four

5.title: CI with GitHub Actions
5.md:
- Workflow anatomy: `on` events, jobs, steps, runners, `needs`, contexts/expressions
- Service containers (Postgres in CI), caching (`actions/cache`, setup-python cache),
  matrix builds, artifacts, concurrency groups
- Secrets vs variables; why fork PRs don't get secrets
- Quality gates: ruff/lint, `pytest` with coverage threshold (career plan: ≥70%),
  build the image, trivy scan
- Running locally with `act` (install it here); `gh run view --log-failed`
- Errors to practice: a job that passes locally but fails in CI (missing env / service
  not healthy), a cache that never hits (wrong key), YAML indentation turning a step
  into something else
- Project: CI for the Phase 3 app — lint + tests against a Postgres service container +
  coverage gate + image build + scan; green under `act` and on GitHub

6.title: Continuous Delivery
6.md:
- Build once, deploy many: push to GHCR, tags (`sha-<short>`, semver), promoting the
  same image across environments
- Environments + required reviewers; deploying via SSH + `docker compose pull && up -d`
  to a VPS (or to [[AWS]] on the emulator once that vault's underway)
- Database migrations in a deploy: ordering, backward-compatible (expand/contract)
  migrations, what happens to old containers mid-deploy
- Rollback = redeploy previous tag; practice it before you need it
- Errors to practice: deploy succeeds, app crashes on start (missing env in prod), a
  migration that locks a big table, pulling `latest` and getting yesterday's image
- Project: push to `main` → image in GHCR → deployed; one rehearsed rollback, timed

7.title: Reliable Deploys & Supply Chain
7.md:
- Zero-downtime: rolling vs blue/green vs canary; health/readiness checks; a reverse
  proxy (Caddy/nginx) switching upstreams
- 12-factor config; log aggregation basics (stdout → collector)
- Supply chain: pin actions by commit SHA, least-privilege `permissions:` block, OIDC
  to cloud instead of long-lived keys, SBOM (`syft`), signing (`cosign`) as a preview,
  Dependabot/Renovate
- Errors to practice: a blue/green switch while the new version isn't ready (dropped
  requests — measure them), a workflow with `permissions: write-all` exploited by a

0.title: Setup
0.md:
- **Time-box / lane:** ~2 h fast lane — test-out gate first (`fast-lane-protocol.md`)
