1.title: Basics
1.md:
- **Time-box / lane:** ~4 h fast lane — test-out gate first (`fast-lane-protocol.md`)
- Types, `:=` vs `var`, control flow — **no `while`, no ternary operator**, both
  deliberate design choices worth naming as such, not gaps
- Functions, multiple return values, zero values (every type has one — no
  "uninitialized" the way C leaves it)
- Functions as values — a function assigned to a variable, passed as an argument, or
  returned from another function is a **Higher-Order Function** the same way it is
  in [[Python]]/[[JavaScript]]; name it explicitly here rather than only meeting it
  later as "just how `sort.Slice`'s comparator works"
- Errors to practice: `panic: runtime error: index out of range` (deliberately trigger
  one, read the stack trace bottom-up like a C segfault), nil-map write panic
  (`assignment to entry in nil map` — a map's zero value is usable for reads, not
  writes, a real gotcha)
- Project: a CLI-style program (`go run`) with real multi-return-value error handling
  from the start, e.g. a small parser that returns `(result, error)` throughout

2.title: Composite Types
2.md:
- **Time-box / lane:** ~6 h fast lane — test-out gate first (`fast-lane-protocol.md`)
- Arrays vs slices — mechanism anchor: a slice header is **3 words** (pointer, length,
  capacity), not a full copy of the data; `append`'s reslicing and capacity-growth
  behavior
- Maps, structs
- Efficiency: slice `append`'s amortized growth is the exact same pattern [[DSA]] Phase
  2 teaches for a dynamic array's doubling strategy — name the connection if that
  vault's been touched. State the amortized cost, don't just say "it's fast."
- Errors to practice: two slices sharing the same underlying array unexpectedly (a
  mutation through one slice silently shows up in the other — no error, wrong
  behavior), a map iteration order assumption (Go deliberately randomizes it — code
  that assumes stable order is a latent bug, not obviously wrong until it runs twice)
- Project: implement a small slice-backed data structure (e.g. a ring buffer or a
  simple stack) from scratch, with a `_test.go` covering the capacity-growth boundary

3.title: Errors, Not Exceptions
3.md:
- **Time-box / lane:** ~5 h fast lane — test-out gate first (`fast-lane-protocol.md`)
- Explicit `error` returns, `if err != nil` as the actual control-flow idiom (not
  boilerplate to skim past), wrapping with `%w` + `errors.Is`/`errors.As`
- `panic`/`recover` as the genuine exception — for truly unrecoverable state, not
  everyday control flow. Direct contrast: every prior language in this set used
  try/catch as the default error-handling shape; Go rejects that on purpose
- Errors to practice: comparing a wrapped error with `==` instead of `errors.Is` (no
  error, silently wrong — the comparison just always fails), a genuinely uncaught
  `panic` crashing the whole program (deliberately trigger one without `recover`, read
  the crash output)
- **Fun project (optional, alongside the graded project below): "Error Chain
  Detective."** Comparing a wrapped error with `==` instead of `errors.Is` is the #1
  real Go mistake — build then debug it instead of just being warned about it. Build
  a 3-4-layer wrapped-error pipeline, plant a deliberate `==`-comparison bug in it,
  hand it to yourself later (or a friend) and trace the wrong comparison using
  `errors.Is`/`errors.As` like a detective story, not a code review.
- Project: a small file-processing tool with a custom error type, wrapped errors
  through at least two layers, and a `recover`-guarded goroutine boundary

4.title: Methods, Interfaces, Composition
4.md:
- **Time-box / lane:** ~9 h fast lane — test-out gate first (`fast-lane-protocol.md`)
- Methods on types, no inheritance — **implicit interface satisfaction**: a type never
  declares "implements X," it just has the right methods. Prove it: define an
  interface after a type that already satisfies it, unchanged.
- Embedding as composition-over-inheritance
- **Generics (type parameters, Go 1.18+)** — Go shipped over a decade without these
  (see `paradigms.md`'s "no generics until 1.18" framing for why); now that they
  exist: type parameters, constraints (`comparable` and beyond), when a generic
  function is actually clearer than an `interface{}`/`any` one and when it isn't
- **Design patterns, already mostly here under other names — make them explicit:**
  Adapter is just implicit interface satisfaction applied to a type you don't own
  (wrap it, satisfy the interface your code expects); Dependency Injection is Go's
  own idiom of "interfaces at the boundary" (formalized fully in Phase 8) — a
  constructor/function takes an interface parameter, not a concrete type
- **Fun project (optional, alongside the graded project below): "Nil Detective."**
  The typed-nil gotcha needs to be seen to be believed (already flagged below) —
  turn it into predict-then-verify puzzles instead of one demo. A dozen short
  snippets assigning various nil pointers/concrete-typed nils/plain `nil` into
  `interface{}`/named-interface variables — predict `== nil` true or false for each
  BEFORE running, see exactly which pattern breaks the intuition.
- Mechanism anchor — **interface representation**: `iface` (2 words: itab pointer +
  data pointer) for interfaces with methods, `eface` (type pointer + data pointer) for
  `interface{}`/`any`. The itab holds the method table — **this IS dynamic dispatch
  here**, contrast directly with [[C-Cpp]] Phase 6's per-object vtable pointer
- Errors to practice: the classic **"typed nil" gotcha** — a nil pointer of a concrete
  type assigned to an interface is NOT a nil interface (`iface != nil` even though the
  underlying pointer is nil) — this one needs to be seen to be believed, trigger it
  deliberately
- Project: a small plugin-style system (e.g. multiple types satisfying one
  `Processor` interface, dispatched through it) with a compile-time assertion
  (`var _ Processor = (*MyType)(nil)`) proving satisfaction before runtime ever checks

5.title: Pointers & Escape Analysis
5.md:
- **Time-box / lane:** ~5 h fast lane — test-out gate first (`fast-lane-protocol.md`)
- Value vs pointer receivers — when each is correct, not just which "feels right"
- Mechanism anchor — **see it, don't guess it**: `go build -gcflags="-m"` prints
  exactly what escapes to the heap and why. This directly extends [[C-Cpp]] Phase 2's
  stack/heap model with empirical proof instead of a mental model alone.
- Errors to practice: a value receiver silently not mutating what the caller expected
  (no error, wrong behavior — the method ran on a copy)
- Project: take a Phase 4 type, write it with both a value-receiver and a
  pointer-receiver method set, run `-gcflags="-m"` on both, explain every escape
  decision that differs

6.title: Concurrency
6.md:
- **Time-box / lane:** ~12 h fast lane — test-out gate first (`fast-lane-protocol.md`)
- Goroutines, channels, `select`, `sync.WaitGroup`/`sync.Mutex`
- Mechanism anchor — **the GMP scheduler**: G (goroutine) / M (OS thread) / P (logical
  processor, holds a local run queue). Goroutines are cheap because their stacks start
  around 2KB and grow, unlike OS threads; work-stealing between P's local queues is
  what makes it scale. `GODEBUG=schedtrace=1000` or `go tool trace` to see it, not just
  read about it.
- Efficiency: goroutine memory cost — thousands of ~2KB-stack goroutines fit where a
  handful of MB-stack OS threads would exhaust memory. State the actual numbers, don't
  just say "goroutines are lightweight."
- Errors to practice: deadlock (`fatal error: all goroutines are asleep - deadlock!` —
  deliberately trigger one, e.g. an unbuffered channel send with no receiver), a data
  race caught by `go test -race` (run without `-race` first — does it "work"? that's
  the trap; then run with `-race` and see what it actually finds)
- **Fun project (optional, alongside the graded project below): "Goroutine Race
  Visualizer."** Goroutines/channels are Go's signature hard-but-cool feature — watch
  them work instead of just reading about them. Build a terminal dashboard with live
  per-goroutine progress bars updating concurrently via channels reporting progress,
  plus a "break it" mode that deliberately deadlocks so `fatal error: all goroutines
  are asleep` happens on screen in real time, not just in a description.
- Project: a small worker pool (goroutines + buffered channel + `WaitGroup`) processing
  a batch of jobs, with a `-race`-clean test proving no data races

7.title: Standard Library & Tooling
7.md:
- **Time-box / lane:** ~6 h fast lane — test-out gate first (`fast-lane-protocol.md`)
- `net/http`, `encoding/json`, `context` for cancellation/timeouts, structured logging
- `slices`/`maps`/`cmp` (Go 1.21+) — the closest thing Go has to a functional stdlib:
  generic `slices.Sort`/`slices.Contains`, `maps.Keys`/`maps.Values`, instead of
  hand-writing the same loop for the tenth time
- Errors to practice: a `context` not propagated into a goroutine, causing a goroutine
  leak (the request finishes but the goroutine keeps running — no crash, just a slow
  resource leak, another "silence isn't proof" case)
- Project: a small HTTP handler using `context` for a timeout, with a test proving the
  handler actually respects cancellation instead of just accepting the parameter

8.title: Testing & Project Structure
8.md:
- **Time-box / lane:** ~6 h fast lane — test-out gate first (`fast-lane-protocol.md`)
- Table-driven tests — Go's own idiom, worth contrasting with [[Python]]'s `pytest`
  `parametrize` if that vault's been touched (same idea, different syntax shape)
- Benchmarks (`go test -bench`), `go doc`, multi-package project layout, interfaces-at-
  the-boundary as Go's version of dependency injection (no DI framework needed — pass
  an interface, swap the implementation in tests)
- Errors to practice: a benchmark that looks fast but isn't measuring what you think
  (compiler optimizing away unused work — the benchmark equivalent of a silently wrong
  answer)
- Project: convert Phase 3's file-processing tool into a proper multi-package layout
  with table-driven tests and one benchmark

9.title: Master / Capstone
9.md:
- **Time-box / lane:** ~18 h fast lane — test-out gate first (`fast-lane-protocol.md`)
- **This is the "cracked at Go" project** — the real test, not another exercise. A
  scoped version is genuinely attemptable right after Phase 6 (concurrency itself,
  since the capstone requires it) — doesn't need Phase 8's formal testing patterns
  first. Don't wait for Phase 9 to exist as a concept before finding out where you
  actually stand.
- A small concurrent backend forcing the GMP model + interfaces + error handling
  together, not learned as isolated boilerplate: a job queue, a rate limiter, a
  scaled-down key-value store built on channels, or a **Task Scheduler with a
  dependency graph** — tasks carry a priority (`container/heap`-backed priority
  queue) and can depend on other tasks (a DAG, resolved via topological sort before
  scheduling), a worker pool (extends Phase 6's project directly) executes ready
  tasks, and cancelling a task cascades via `context` cancellation to everything that
  depends on it — the one project here that forces the priority-queue/topo-sort
  algorithms [[DSA]] teaches separately into one coherent running system
- Errors to practice: whatever the capstone's own concurrency shape produces for real —
  by now this should need no prompting
- Capstone: ship something runnable end to end, `-race`-clean, tested, with real error
  handling throughout — not a toy that only works under the happy path

10.title: Maverick
10.md:
- **Time-box / lane:** optional, uncounted

Master proves you're solid across the whole language. Maverick is a chosen
specialization on top of that — pick a track (or several), not all are required.
Tracks below are ordered easiest/smallest-scope → hardest/largest-scope; each track's
project sits at the same bar as Phase 9's capstone, not another exercise.

### Track A — CLI Tooling at Scale
- Cobra command tree: subcommands, persistent flags vs local flags, command
  composition
- Plugin architecture: discovering and loading external binaries/subcommands at
  runtime (the pattern `kubectl` plugins and `git` subcommands both use — an
  executable named `toolname-subcmd` on `PATH`)
- Cross-compilation (`GOOS`/`GOARCH` matrix) and a real release pipeline
  (`goreleaser`) — one `go build` invocation isn't a release
- Errors to practice: a flag-parsing conflict between a persistent and local flag
  with the same name (silently picks one, no error — read Cobra's precedence rules
  instead of guessing), a cross-compiled binary that panics only on one target OS
  because of a platform-specific stdlib difference
- Project: a real multi-command CLI (Cobra) with at least one externally-loadable
  plugin subcommand, built and released for 3 OS/arch targets via a `goreleaser`
  config
- No dedicated course in the library — nothing to point to. Cobra's own docs and
  `goreleaser`'s docs are the primary source here

### Track B — Systems Observability
- Structured metrics: counters/gauges/histograms, what each actually measures and
  when a histogram beats an average (tail latency hides in an average)
- A Prometheus exporter: `/metrics` endpoint, exposition format, label cardinality
  (why unbounded labels are a real production incident, not a style nitpick)
- OpenTelemetry: traces vs metrics vs logs as three different signals, context
  propagation across goroutines/service boundaries (Phase 7's `context` habit, now
  carrying a trace ID instead of just a deadline)
- Errors to practice: a high-cardinality label that silently blows up a metrics
  backend's memory (no error in your code — the damage shows up somewhere else
  entirely), a trace missing a span because context wasn't propagated into a
  spawned goroutine (Phase 7's leak lesson, now showing up as a broken trace instead
  of a leaked goroutine)
- Project: instrument Phase 9's capstone (or a scoped service) with Prometheus
  metrics and OpenTelemetry tracing, scrape it, and show a trace that follows one
  request across at least two goroutine boundaries
- No dedicated course in the library — nothing to point to. Prometheus/OpenTelemetry's
  own docs are the primary source

### Track C — High-Performance Networking
- Raw TCP: `net.Listen`, connection handling, why a naive one-goroutine-per-connection
  model is fine until it isn't (ties directly to Phase 6's goroutine-cost numbers)
- A protocol implemented from scratch (framing, length-prefixed messages — the
  "where does one message end" problem every raw-TCP protocol has to solve)
- A reverse proxy or load balancer: connection pooling, backend health checks, why
  "just forward the bytes" gets complicated fast
- Errors to practice: a partial read/write on a TCP socket (a `net.Conn` doesn't
  guarantee one `Write` call arrives as one `Read` on the other end — the framing
  problem showing up as a bug instead of a design constraint), a
  goroutine-per-connection leak from a connection that's half-closed and never
  cleaned up
- Project: a small TCP proxy or load balancer with a real framed protocol,
  health-checked backends, and a `-race`-clean test proving no goroutine leaks under
  a connection-churn test
- No dedicated course in the library — nothing to point to. Go's own `net` package
  docs and reading a real proxy's source are the primary source

### Track D — Security
- mTLS: certificate generation, mutual verification (both sides prove identity, not
  just the server), why service-to-service auth in a mesh leans on this instead of
  API keys
- Writing a security scanner: a port scanner or a TLS-config auditor (weak cipher
  suites, expired/self-signed certs) — something that inspects a target, not just
  talks to it
- Errors to practice: a TLS handshake failure from a certificate chain that's valid
  but not trusted by the verifying side (reading `x509: certificate signed by
  unknown authority` and knowing which side's trust store is missing the CA), a
  scanner false negative from a closed-but-filtered port reported as "closed" when
  it's actually silently dropped
- Project: an mTLS-secured client/server pair (self-signed CA, generated certs,
  mutual verification enforced — not just TLS enabled), plus a small scanner tool
  run against a target you control
- No dedicated course in the library — nothing to point to. Go's own `crypto/tls`/
  `crypto/x509` docs are the primary source

### Track E — Distributed Systems / Microservices
- gRPC + Protobuf: schema-first service definitions, unary vs streaming RPCs, why a
  `.proto` contract beats a hand-maintained REST API doc for service-to-service calls
- Service discovery: how a client finds a service instance when there's more than
  one, without a hardcoded address
- Distributed tracing across service boundaries — extends Track B's OpenTelemetry
  work if both are picked, now propagating a trace ID over gRPC metadata instead of
  within one process
- Errors to practice: a gRPC deadline not propagated to a downstream call (the
  request "succeeds" from the caller's view but the downstream keeps working past
  when anyone's still waiting — Phase 7's context-cancellation lesson at a
  distributed scale), a Protobuf schema change that breaks an old client silently
  (wire-compatible but semantically wrong — no error, wrong behavior, the hardest
  kind again)
- Project: two or more small gRPC services calling each other, with propagated
  deadlines/tracing across the call, and one deliberately-introduced
  schema-evolution scenario handled without breaking the older service
- No dedicated course in the library — nothing to point to. `grpc.io`'s official Go
  docs are the primary source

### Track F — Cloud-Native Infra Tooling
- Largest scope of any track here — a real Kubernetes ecosystem to learn on top of
  Go itself, not just more Go
- The Kubernetes API machinery: informers/listers (a local cache kept in sync with
  the cluster, not a poll-on-demand), the reconciliation-loop pattern (a controller
  doesn't "handle an event," it repeatedly asks "what should this look like, what
  does it look like, fix the difference")
- `client-go` (or a higher-level framework like controller-runtime/kubebuilder) to
  build a real custom controller watching a custom resource
- Errors to practice: an informer cache that's briefly stale (the reconciliation
  loop's whole design assumes this and self-corrects — seeing a controller act on
  stale data and converge anyway is the actual lesson, not a bug to fix), a reconcile
  loop that isn't idempotent and does something twice on a re-run (retries are the
  normal case in this model, not the exception)
- Project: a small custom controller (client-go or controller-runtime) watching a
  custom resource and reconciling real cluster state to match it — deployed and
  demonstrably self-healing after a manual state change
- No Go-specific course in the library. The generic (non-Go)
  `~/ElementalMedia/Courses/Git Docker kubernetes/[TutsNode.net] - Complete
  Kubernetes Tutorial` and `.../CodeWithMosh - The Ultimate Docker Course` cover the
  platform concepts (pods/controllers/reconciliation from the ops side) this track
  needs as background, but neither touches `client-go`/writing a controller itself —
  not content-verified against this track, folder names only

0.title: Setup
0.md:
- **Time-box / lane:** ~2 h fast lane — test-out gate first (`fast-lane-protocol.md`)
- Node.js + npm/pnpm, browser DevTools console
- A bundler-free starting point: `<script type="module">`, no build step yet
- Editor/LSP wired up
- Project: none — environment readiness check

1.title: Basics
1.md:
- **Time-box / lane:** ~3 h fast lane — test-out gate first (`fast-lane-protocol.md`)
- `let`/`const` and the temporal dead zone (why `var` is the wrong default, not just
  the old one), types & coercion, operators, control flow, functions, template literals
- Errors to practice: `ReferenceError` from a TDZ violation (reading a `let` before its
  declaration line), `TypeError: undefined is not a function` (calling something that
  isn't callable — read which identifier it's complaining about)
- Project: a small CLI-style script run via `node` (e.g. a unit converter or FizzBuzz
  variant) with real type coercion edge cases handled deliberately, not accidentally

2.title: Core Data Structures
2.md:
- **Time-box / lane:** ~6 h fast lane — test-out gate first (`fast-lane-protocol.md`)
- Arrays, objects, `Map`/`Set` (and when each beats a plain object — key types, insertion
  order guarantees, iteration), destructuring, spread/rest, JSON
- Cross-link: same "how is this actually stored" question as [[Python]] Phase 2's
  dict/list framing and [[DSA]]'s array/hash-table content — name the connection if
  either's been touched
- Efficiency: array index access is O(1), `Array.prototype.includes`/`indexOf` are
  O(n); `Map`/`Set` lookup is ~O(1) via hashing, same trade-off DSA's hash tables teach.
  V8 footnote: keeping an object's shape consistent (not adding/deleting properties ad
  hoc after creation) lets the engine optimize property access via hidden classes —
  why two "identical-looking" objects can perform differently.
- Errors to practice: `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined` (the single most
  common real-world JS error — reading a property off something that turned out to be
  `undefined`/`null`), silently wrong output from comparing objects/arrays with `===`
  (reference equality, not structural — no error, wrong behavior)
- Project: a small data-processing script (parse a JSON array of records, group/
  aggregate with `Map`, produce a summary) — no library shortcut, raw language only

3.title: Functions & Scope
3.md:
- **Time-box / lane:** ~8 h fast lane — test-out gate first (`fast-lane-protocol.md`)
- Closures as **actual retained scope objects** — not "the function remembers stuff,"
  a closure keeps a live reference to its outer scope's variable binding. Canonical
  proof: `var` vs `let` in a loop with `setTimeout` — predict the output before running
- `this` binding: the four rules (default/implicit/explicit/`new`) plus arrow
  functions' lexical `this` as the exception — resolved by the call site, not the
  definition site (except arrows)
- Higher-order functions, `arguments` vs rest params
- Errors to practice: `this` silently being `undefined`/wrong-object (no error, wrong
  behavior — a callback losing its bound `this`), `RangeError: Maximum call stack size
  exceeded` from unbounded recursion
- **Fun project (optional, alongside the graded project below): "`this` Detective."**
  `this`-binding is the other classic JS interview-question nightmare besides the
  event loop — turn it into short predict-then-verify puzzles instead of a rules
  list to memorize. A dozen short snippets (arrow vs regular function, `bind`/`call`/
  `apply`, an event handler, a method passed as a callback) — guess what `this` is
  BEFORE running each one, score yourself, see which rule you actually don't have
  yet instead of assuming you do.
- Project: an event-callback-style module (e.g. a simple pub/sub or observer) where a
  `this`-binding bug is deliberately introduced and fixed, plus a closure-based counter
  factory

4.title: Prototypes & OOP
4.md:
- **Time-box / lane:** ~9 h fast lane — test-out gate first (`fast-lane-protocol.md`)
- The prototype chain: `Object.getPrototypeOf()`/`Object.create()`, walking a chain by
  hand before ever using `class`
- `class` syntax as **confirmed sugar over prototypes, not a separate mechanism** —
  prove it: `typeof MyClass === 'function'`, inspect `MyClass.prototype`
- `Object.freeze`, getters/setters
- **Fun project (optional, alongside the graded project below): "Prototype Chain
  Explorer."** Confusing for anyone coming from a class-based language — make the
  chain visible instead of assumed. Each round: an increasingly weird object (deep
  `Object.create` chain, a `class` instance, a plain literal, `null`-prototype
  object) — predict its FULL prototype chain end to end before checking with
  `Object.getPrototypeOf()` in a loop, see exactly where the guess breaks.
- **Design patterns, named explicitly:** Adapter (a wrapper object exposing the
  interface your code expects over something that doesn't natively have it) —
  Dependency Injection (pass a dependency in as a constructor/function argument
  instead of importing it directly inside — swap it for a test double without
  touching the class; direct parallel to [[Python]]'s `Protocol`-typed constructors
  and [[C-Cpp]]'s base-class-pointer constructors)
- Errors to practice: `TypeError: X is not a constructor` (calling a non-constructor
  with `new`, or forgetting `new` entirely), a prototype-chain lookup miss returning
  `undefined` instead of throwing (no error — the classic "why is this property just
  missing" JS trap)
- Project: build the same small type hierarchy twice — once with raw
  `Object.create`/prototype wiring, once with `class` — confirm they produce
  identical `Object.getPrototypeOf()` chains

5.title: Asynchronous JavaScript
5.md:
- **Time-box / lane:** ~10 h fast lane — test-out gate first (`fast-lane-protocol.md`)
- Callbacks → Promises → `async`/`await` as **the same mechanism at three syntax
  layers**, not three unrelated topics — show the same operation written all three ways
- The event loop: call stack, Web/Node APIs, macrotask queue, **microtask queue fully
  drains between every macrotask** — this ordering rule is the single most-tested
  mechanism question in this phase
- Efficiency: microtask starvation is a *speed* bug, not just an async-correctness one
  — a runaway `.then()` chain that keeps queuing more microtasks can starve the
  render/macrotask queue entirely, freezing a page that never throws an error
- Errors to practice: an unhandled promise rejection (silent by default in many
  environments — deliberately trigger one and notice how quietly it fails), and the
  classic mispredict — log `setTimeout(fn, 0)` vs `Promise.resolve().then(fn)` together
  and predict the order before running
- **Fun project (optional, alongside the graded project below): "Race the Event
  Loop."** The event loop is the most commonly cited "wait, why does THAT run first"
  JS gotcha — turn the confusion into a scored game. Build a page that generates a
  random mix of `setTimeout`/`Promise.then()`/sync calls, has the player predict the
  full execution order BEFORE running it, scores the guess, and animates the actual
  call-stack/microtask/macrotask queues live so the reveal is visual, not just a log.
- Project: fetch/simulate 3 async operations, implemented once with raw callbacks, once
  with `.then()` chains, once with `async`/`await` — same behavior, three syntax layers

6.title: The DOM & Browser APIs
6.md:
- **Time-box / lane:** ~6 h fast lane — test-out gate first (`fast-lane-protocol.md`)
- DOM traversal/mutation, events (bubbling, capturing, delegation — and why delegation
  is usually the right call for dynamic lists)
- `fetch`, browser storage (`localStorage`/`sessionStorage`)
- Errors to practice: a DOM query that silently returns `null` (element not found,
  wrong selector or timing) then crashes two lines later on `.textContent` — the null
  check that should have been there
- Project: a small interactive page (e.g. a filterable list or a simple form with
  live validation) using event delegation, no framework

7.title: Modules & Tooling
7.md:
- **Time-box / lane:** ~5 h fast lane — test-out gate first (`fast-lane-protocol.md`)
- ESM vs CommonJS — what actually differs (static vs dynamic imports, `this`/top-level
  `await` availability), why they don't always interop cleanly
- Bundlers (Vite/esbuild) at a conceptual level — what a bundler is actually solving
- `package.json`, npm dependency resolution, why `node_modules` looks the way it does
- Built-ins survey — reach for these instead of reinventing them: `Date` (and why raw
  `Date` math is a well-known footgun — timezone/DST edge cases), `RegExp`, `Math`;
  on the Node side, `fs` (file I/O) and `path` (never string-concatenate a path by
  hand, `path.join` handles the platform differences)
- Errors to practice: `SyntaxError: Cannot use import statement outside a module` /
  `require is not defined in ES module scope` — the two-sided ESM/CJS interop error,
  diagnosing which side the mismatch is on
- Project: split Phase 6's page into ES modules, add a minimal Vite config, confirm it
  builds and runs both in dev mode and as a production build

8.title: Testing & Node Backend
8.md:
- **Time-box / lane:** ~7 h fast lane — test-out gate first (`fast-lane-protocol.md`)
- Vitest/Jest: assertions, mocking, async test patterns
- Node's module/HTTP/fs basics, npm scripts
- Errors to practice: an async test that times out because a returned promise was
  never awaited by the test itself, and reading a raw test-runner failure diff
  (expected vs actual) the same rigor as any other assertion output
- Project: a minimal Node HTTP server (no framework) with a test suite covering at
  least one success path and one error path

9.title: TypeScript
9.md:
- **Time-box / lane:** ~10 h fast lane — test-out gate first (`fast-lane-protocol.md`)
- **Mechanism anchor**: TS types are compile-time-only — erased at runtime. Prove it:
  compile a `.ts` file, diff the emitted `.js` against the source. No type annotation
  survives. **Structural typing, not nominal** — two differently-named types with the
  same shape satisfy each other; worth contrasting with [[C-Cpp]]'s nominal typing if
  that vault's been touched (see its `tutorials/paradigms.md`)
- `tsconfig.json` and what `strict` actually turns on, basic types, interfaces vs type
  aliases, generics, type narrowing (union types + control-flow analysis), utility
  types (`Partial`/`Pick`/`Omit`), `any` vs `unknown` (`any` is a hole in the type
  system, not a convenience), `.d.ts` files for JS interop
- Pragmatic Paranoia tie-in: TS's type system IS design-by-contract enforced by the
  compiler instead of by convention — see
  `~/ElementalMedia/Projects/pragmatic-programmer.md`
- Efficiency: types are a compile-time-only cost, zero runtime overhead — worth stating
  explicitly, "does TypeScript make my code slower" is a common wrong intuition
- Errors to practice: `TS2322`-class type-mismatch errors (read which two types are
  actually being compared, not just "it's wrong"), the silent safety-loss of `any`
  spreading through a codebase (no error, no protection either — same "silence isn't
  proof" pattern as everywhere else in this vault). Direct comparison exercise: take a
  Phase 2/3 bug that surfaced as a runtime `TypeError`, add types with `strict` on,
  watch the compiler catch the same bug before ever running the code.
- Project: take the Phase 8 Node HTTP server, convert it to TypeScript with `strict`
  mode on, fix every compiler error surfaced — no `any` anywhere in the final version
  unless a comment justifies why nothing narrower fits.

10.title: Master / Capstone
10.md:
- **Time-box / lane:** ~18 h fast lane — test-out gate first (`fast-lane-protocol.md`)
- **This is the "cracked at JavaScript" project** — the real test, not another
  tutorial-follow-along. A scoped plain-interactive-page version (no framework) is
  genuinely attemptable right after Phase 6 (DOM); the fuller React/full-stack flavor
  wants Phase 9 (TypeScript) too. Don't wait for Phase 10 to exist as a concept before
  finding out where you actually stand.
- A small full-stack app, one frontend framework (React) applied **on top of owned
  fundamentals**, not learned as a black box — every hook/pattern should map back to a
  mechanism already understood (closures, the event loop, prototypes) — or a **URL
  Shortener**: a small Node backend that hash/base62-encodes a counter to a short
  code, handles collisions, and stores the mapping behind an Adapter/Gateway-shaped
  object (Phase 4's patterns) so the backing store is swappable without touching the
  routing code — a genuinely different systems-design shape than a frontend-
  framework capstone. Building whichever in TypeScript is encouraged now that
  Phase 9's behind you, not required.
- Errors to practice: whatever the capstone's own stack produces for real — by now this
  should need no prompting
- Capstone: ship something runnable end to end — a small full-stack app, or a
  from-scratch feature in React/Vue built with the fundamentals explicit, not copied
  from a tutorial

11.title: Maverick
11.md:
- **Time-box / lane:** optional, uncounted

Master proves you're solid across the whole language. Maverick is a chosen
specialization on top of that — pick a track (or several), not all are required.
Tracks below are ordered easiest/smallest-scope → hardest/largest-scope; each track's
project sits at the same bar as Phase 10's capstone, not another exercise.

### Track A — State Management & Frontend Performance
- Redux Toolkit / global state patterns beyond component-local state — when state
  actually needs to be global vs prop-drilled/lifted
- Memoization: `React.memo`, `useMemo`/`useCallback`, and when they're a net loss
  (reference-equality cost vs the render they'd skip)
- Virtualization for long lists (windowing — render only visible rows)
- Core Web Vitals: LCP/FID/CLS, Chrome DevTools Performance tab, profiling a real
  render waterfall instead of guessing
- Errors to practice: an infinite re-render loop from a `useEffect` dependency mistake
  (a hang/freeze, not a clean error — Phase 5's event-loop "silence isn't proof"
  lesson recurring in React's render cycle), a `useMemo`/`useCallback` that "fixes"
  nothing because the dependency array itself is unstable (a new object literal every
  render)
- Project: take Phase 10's React capstone (if built), add global state with Redux,
  profile a slow list render, fix it with virtualization + memoization, show
  before/after numbers
- Course: `[FreeCoursesOnline.Me] Code With Mosh - The Ultimate Redux Course`
  (already cited at Ph10)

### Track B — GraphQL
- Schema design: types, queries, mutations, resolvers — the request/response shape
  GraphQL trades for REST's URL-per-resource model
- Client-side integration: fetching, caching, and why a GraphQL client
  (Apollo/urql) does more work than `fetch` for the same request
- Errors to practice: a resolver that silently returns `null` for a nested field with
  no top-level error (a partial-response shape — GraphQL's own "no error, wrong data"
  pattern, distinct from REST's all-or-nothing failure), an N+1 query problem across
  resolvers (correct output, terrible performance — the same efficiency habit as
  every other phase, now at the resolver level)
- Project: a small GraphQL API (schema + resolvers) backing a client component that
  queries it, with one deliberately-introduced N+1 fixed via batching (DataLoader
  pattern)
- Course: `~/ElementalMedia/Courses/web/Frontendmasters - Client-Side GraphQL in
  React [AhLaN]` — not content-verified against this track yet, folder name only

### Track C — Testing/QA at Scale
- E2E testing (Playwright/Cypress): a real browser driven end-to-end, distinct from
  Phase 8's unit-level Vitest/Jest
- Visual regression testing, contract testing (an API's consumer and producer agree
  on shape without a shared integration environment)
- Errors to practice: a flaky E2E test (passes/fails inconsistently — timing-
  dependent, the hardest category of test bug to actually fix rather than just retry
  away), a visual-regression false positive from an unrelated font-rendering
  difference
- Project: an E2E suite for Phase 10's capstone covering the main user flow, plus one
  contract test between its frontend and backend if the capstone has both
- No dedicated E2E/Playwright/Cypress course in the library — nothing to point to
  directly. `[FreeCoursesOnline.Me] FrontendMasters - Enterprise UI Development
  Testing & Code Quality` (already cited at Ph8) is the closest existing anchor

### Track D — Web Security
- XSS: reflected vs stored vs DOM-based, why `innerHTML` with untrusted input is the
  canonical mistake
- CSRF: same-site cookies, tokens, why "the request came from a logged-in browser"
  isn't proof it came from your own page

1.title: Pitch & Time
1.md:
- **Time-box / lane:** ~6 h fast lane — test-out gate first (`fast-lane-protocol.md`)
- **Mechanism anchor:** pitch = frequency; an octave is a 2:1 ratio; 12-TET splits it into 12 equal steps of 2^(1/12); MIDI note number 69 = A4 = 440 Hz, and `f = 440 · 2^((n−69)/12)`.
- Notes, accidentals, enharmonics, the keyboard layout (7 white + 5 black) and the same notes on the guitar fretboard; staff and clefs; note names ↔ MIDI numbers ↔ frequencies.
- Rhythm: beat, tempo (BPM), meter (4/4, 3/4, 6/8), subdivision, rests, ties, dotted notes, triplets, swing. Quantize and the grid.
- Course: *Music Theory for Songwriters* — "the octave", "seven white notes and five black notes".
- Project: `theory.py` pitch layer — `note_to_midi()`, `midi_to_freq()`, `transpose()` (pitch-class arithmetic mod 12), enharmonic-aware spelling; plus a click track and a 4/4 vs 6/8 pattern in LMMS/Hydrogen.
- Errors: A♯ vs B♭ spelling, off-by-one in mod 12, octave-number off by one (C4 vs C3 between tools), off-grid notes, tempo-vs-meter confusion.

2.title: Scales, Intervals, Keys
2.md:
- **Time-box / lane:** ~10 h fast lane — test-out gate first (`fast-lane-protocol.md`)
- **Mechanism anchor:** a major scale is the step pattern W-W-H-W-W-W-H; every other scale is a rotation or alteration of a step pattern; an interval is a semitone count *plus* a letter distance (so quality is determined by both).
- Intervals: perfect/major/minor/augmented/diminished, inversion, consonance vs dissonance (ratio intuition). Course: "intervals", "figuring out intervals".
- Keys and key signatures, relative major/minor, the circle of fifths/fourths, parallel vs relative keys.
- Minor: natural / harmonic / melodic; modes (Ionian→Locrian) as rotations of the major scale and their mood; pentatonic and blues scales (and their guitar boxes).
- Project: `scale()` / `interval()` / `key_signature()` generator + self-check; the same 8-bar melody in four modes in LMMS; mode→mood table from your own ears.
- Errors: wrong interval quality (major vs perfect), mixing sharps and flats in one scale, wrong relative minor, hearing a mode as "just a different scale".

3.title: Chords & Functional Harmony
3.md:
- **Time-box / lane:** ~12 h fast lane — test-out gate first (`fast-lane-protocol.md`)
- **Mechanism anchor:** a chord is stacked scale degrees (every other note); diatonic chords are built from the scale itself; function (tonic / subdominant / dominant) is about tension and resolution, not about the chord's name.
- Triads (major/minor/dim/aug), 7ths, inversions, slash chords; diatonic chords + roman numerals (I ii iii IV V vi vii°); chord function; cadences (authentic, plagal, half, deceptive).
- Common progressions (I–V–vi–IV, ii–V–I, 12-bar blues) and why they work; basic voice leading (smooth motion, common tones).
- Chords on the guitar: open and barre shapes derived from the same patterns.
- Project: `chord()`, `diatonic_chords(key)`, `analyze(progression)` in `theory.py` + progression → MIDI generator (via `mido`), loaded into LMMS and heard.
- Errors: parallel fifths/octaves, unresolved leading tone, spelling a chord with wrong accidentals (C♯–E–G♯ vs D♭–F–A♭ in context), jumpy voicings.

4.title: Melody, Loops & Game Music (Stage 1 capstone)
4.md:
- **Time-box / lane:** ~10 h fast lane — test-out gate first (`fast-lane-protocol.md`)
- Melody: motif, contour, phrase and antecedent/consequent, call-and-response, tension notes vs chord tones, rhythm of a hook.
- Game music craft: **seamless loops** (bar-aligned length, tails and reverb tails, zero-crossing/crossfade), layered/adaptive music (vertical layering vs horizontal re-sequencing), mode→mood mapping, stingers and transitions on a bar line; SFX pitch design (pitch-shift and pitch-randomization from the same scale).
- Drums and groove with Hydrogen/LMMS BeatBox; basic mix (levels, pan, EQ) just enough to export a clean stem.
- Project (capstone): a **60 s looping track + 3 stems (OGG)** in one key, loop seam clean, drop-in for [[GameDev]] Branch C / Phase 4 buses (log in that vault's `ASSETS.md`).
- Efficiency: stem length = whole number of bars at the project tempo, verified by sample count (`wave` module), not by ear alone.
- Errors: click/pop at the loop seam, stems in clashing keys, off-grid hits, clipping (peaks above 0 dBFS), loop that "restarts" audibly because the reverb tail was cut.

5.title: Harmonize a Melody
5.md:
- **Time-box / lane:** ~10 h fast lane — test-out gate first (`fast-lane-protocol.md`)
- Choosing chords from the melody: melody notes as chord tones, passing/neighbor tones, chord-change timing, bass line choices.
- Course: *Songwriting Techniques with Chords* — "Harmonize a Melody".
- Trade-offs: one melody, three harmonizations (plain, rich, surprising) and how each changes the mood.
- Project: harmonize 3 given melodies + one of your own; `analyze()` checks the Roman numerals; guitar-playable chord charts.
- Errors: clash between melody note and chord, too many chord changes, melody always on the chord's root.

6.title: Harmonic Rhythm & Colour
6.md:
- **Time-box / lane:** ~12 h fast lane — test-out gate first (`fast-lane-protocol.md`)

7.title: Form, Lyrics, Arrangement
